issues.title: Cover "Certificate-Bound Access Tokens" part of RFC 8705
issues.author: dagdagdag83
issues.body:
The company that I work for is implementing a workload identity pattern (inspired heavily by WIMSE WG) for securing service to service communication. One of the biggest benefits that we are leveraging is using Istio mTLS certificates (which are roughly SPIFFE-compatible) to get Certificate-Bound Access Tokens. This is something you get for "free" when implementing RFC 8705.

IMO this specification should be more explicit about the ability to get certificate-bound tokens, because in effect these tokens are actually **workload-bound** (via SPIFFE ID) which is a huge security benefit. 

The only modification we'd had to make for RFC 8705 is the following:

1) We add a new cnf claim:
```
  "cnf":{
    "x5t#S256": "87abe78e185a0c5ee193bf1e34b36bbf43f47178850871b30225e23542b7d503",
    "x5s#SPIFFE": "spiffe://cluster.local/ns/namespace/sa/default"
  }
```
The `x5s#SPIFFE` is intended to reference to SPIFFE ID, the reason for that is because istio rotates mTLS certificates very quickly so we didn't want to rely on only the `x5t#S256` claim to validate the binding.

2) RFC 8705 expects that the leaf cert itself or thumbprint is saved (or available at least) to the AS so that it can verify it.
For the same reason as above (rapid rotation) we don't do this. We only store the SPIFFE ID, then we use the root public CA (which Istio publishes) to verify the cert chain itself.

Then following that, any of our APIs that gets these tokens will pretty much validate the certificate-binding per RFC 8705.

comments.author: arndt-s
comments.body:
Hi @dagdagdag83 

sorry for just getting back to you know. We've had a look at the issue and believe it's out of scope for now.

While it seems simple at first, it comes with a lot of security considerations:
- Binding to an identifier instead of a key has caveats and heavily depends on the granularity of the identifier (is it an instance, is it a logical unit, what if the identifier is shared?)
- Resource servers need to change their logic to accept "identifier-bound" access tokens.

However, we acknowledge that we need to talk more about some of the scenarios you mention:
- When SVID key rotates, should the workload request a new AT from the AS?
- What about general keybinding? Should easily be possible for X.509-SVIDs.

issues.title: Client ID for Client Authentication using X509-SVID
issues.author: TakahikoKawasaki
issues.body:
In draft 00 of OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication, when using Client Authentication with X509-SVID, it requires that the value of the `client_id` request parameter be the SPIFFE ID. However, I believe this requirement should be removed. The reasons are as follows:

* Systems that use the [OpenID Federation 1.0](https://openid.net/specs/openid-federation-1_0.html) specification cannot use OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication.
* Systems that use the [OAuth Client ID Metadata Document](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document/) specification cannot use OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication.
* Systems in which client IDs cannot be flexibly changed cannot use OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication.

The client authentication method defined in RFC 8705 [Section 2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8705.html#section-2.1) works correctly even if the value of the `tls_client_auth_san_uri` client metadata differs from the client ID.

comments.author: maganuk
comments.body:
Coincidentally, we had implemented a working version of this before the draft was published, and we are planning to make it public soon.

In our implementation, the OAuth client_id is not required to be the SPIFFE ID. The client_id remains the OAuth client registration identifier, and the SPIFFE URI SAN validation is configured as part of the client’s authentication credential/secret type. In other words, the AS resolves the OAuth client using client_id, validates the presented X.509-SVID, extracts the SPIFFE ID from the URI SAN, and then checks that the SPIFFE ID is associated with that registered client.

We have not implemented the Client ID Metadata Document part yet; this is currently configured directly on the registered client.

From an implementer perspective, requiring client_id == SPIFFE ID feels unnecessarily restrictive. In many deployments, client_id may already be a stable application identifier, while the SPIFFE ID represents a workload/runtime identity. This distinction becomes especially useful for agentic systems, where a single OAuth client registration may represent an agent application, runtime, or class/group of clients, while individual workloads may have distinct SPIFFE IDs.

The validation rule already seems to allow the SPIFFE ID to be “associated with a registered client identifier”. I think the spec would be more deployable if the X.509-SVID section made that association model explicit and did not require the request client_id itself to equal the URI SAN.

issues.title: IANA OAuth Parameters for SPIFFE Client Authentication
issues.author: TakahikoKawasaki
issues.body:
I would like to propose the following [IANA OAuth Parameters](https://www.iana.org/assignments/oauth-parameters/oauth-parameters.xhtml) for SPIFFE Client Authentication:

### OAuth Dynamic Client Registration Metadata

- `spiffe_id`
- `spiffe_bundle_endpoint`

### OAuth Token Endpoint Authentication Methods

- `spiffe_jwt`
-  `spiffe_x509`

### Rationale for spiffe_id

SPIFFE Client Authentication with JWT-SVIDs requires the authorization server to ensure that the SPIFFE ID in the SVID matches the registered value, but the specification does not define how this verification is to be performed. If the `spiffe_id` client metadata is available, the authorization server can satisfy this requirement by comparing the registered metadata value with the SPIFFE ID contained in the SVID.

### Rationale for spiffe_bundle_endpoint

Because the location of the SPIFFE Bundle Endpoint cannot be inferred from the SPIFFE ID or the SVID, it must be preconfigured. However, the specification does not define how this configuration is to be performed. If the `spiffe_bundle_endpoint` client metadata is available, the authorization server can use it to store the preconfigured value.

### Rationale for spiffe_jwt and spiffe_x509

The `token_endpoint_auth_method` client metadata and the `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported` server metadata require identifiers representing the new client authentication methods defined by this specification.

issues.title: Distinguishing between non-SPIFFE and SPIFFE TLS authentication?
issues.author: stianst
issues.body:
`JWT-SVIDs` uses a different `client_assertion_type` making it simple for the authorization server to identify if the client is using a "regular" JWT client assertion or a JWT-SVID.

For `X509-SVID` the only way the authorization server can distinguish between a "regular" mTLS authentication and SPIFFE is by parsing the `client_id`. 

This may lead to difficulty in support in authorization servers. As an example in Keycloak client authentication is implemented as a chain of authenticators, where the first authenticator that is able to authenticate the client is used (with an addition check that once the client is identified the correct authenticator was selected). This effectively means the regular mTLS authenticator would have to have an exclusion if the client_id is prefixed with `spiffe`.

Additionally Keycloak expects the `client_id` parameter to be the ID of the client within Keycloak; and not the SPIFFE SVID.

Would it make sense to use an alternative parameter such as `spiffe_svid` instead of `client_id` to make it clear to the authorization server what it is?

issues.title: spiffe_wit should be independent of attestation-based client authentication
issues.author: TakahikoKawasaki
issues.body:
In the client authentication method using WIT-SVID defined in [draft 01](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-spiffe-client-auth-01.html) of the [OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-spiffe-client-auth/) specification (hereafter referred to as `spiffe_wit`), applying the concepts of [OAuth 2.0 Attestation-Based Client Authentication](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-attestation-based-client-auth/) (hereafter ABCA) is reasonable. However, having it encroach upon the ABCA specification raises the following issues.

- According to the [WIMSE Workload Credentials](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-wimse-workload-creds/) specification, the `sub` claim of a Workload Identity Token (hereafter WIT) must be an identifier of the workload. On the other hand, in ABCA, the `sub` claim of a Client Attestation must be an identifier of the OAuth client. Since a workload and an OAuth client are not necessarily in a one-to-one relationship, using a WIT as a Client Attestation leads to a conflict in the requirements for the `sub` claim.
- In addition, there is an attempt to make ABCA implementations accept `wit+jwt` as a value of the `typ` of a Client Attestation JWT, in addition to `oauth-client-attestation+jwt`.

These issues can be avoided by modifying the specification as follows:

1. Use the `Workload-Identity-Token` HTTP header instead of the `OAuth-Client-Attestation` HTTP header. This header is defined in the WIMSE Workload Credentials specification.
2. Introduce and use a new `Workload-Identity-Token-PoP` HTTP header instead of the `OAuth-Client-Attestation-PoP` HTTP header. (This new header would likely be better defined in the WIMSE Workload Credentials specification rather than in the OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication specification.)

Since a WIT does not contain information identifying the OAuth client, when using the revised `spiffe_wit` client authentication, a separate `client_id` request parameter would be required. The server implementation would then, similar to the case of `spiffe_jwt` client authentication, verify that the value of the `spiffe_id` client metadata parameter of the OAuth client identified by the `client_id` request parameter matches the value of the `sub` claim in the WIT.

comments.body: The comment indicates a certificate mismatch issue between the bundle and the X509-SVID; please verify and update the certificate data to ensure consistency.
"The SPIFFE Bundle Endpoint exposes the signing keys for X509 and JWT-SVIDs over HTTP via a JSON Web Key Set according to {{RFC7517}}."
"Server authentication on this endpoint is available in two flavors. For the sake of interoperability, in context of this specification the WebPKI flavor MUST be used."

On second reading, I think it's fine to put the system trust store in "methods to avoid", and clarify the proper method here. In reference to our offline discussion: This section doesn't say anything about scoping down the trust store. But the client doesn't have the information to know how to do that. That's really up to the bundle endpoint.

"The SPIFFE ID carried in the URI SAN is rarely a verifiable attribute in the broader X.509 ecosystem. Using the system trust store as trust anchor would allow ANY certificate authority in it to issue a trusted X509-SVID for ANY SPIFFE ID."

Instead of:

The authors acknowledge that using the SPIFFE Workload API can reduce the time an update of the bundle is received by the authorization server.

how about:

Using the SPIFFE Workload API reduces the latency between an update to the trust bundle and the time the authorization server receives the update.
Is this a pattern we want to encourage?

This seems overly restrictive - not sure about the "NOT RECOMMENDED" here - I think it comes down to the rust relationships that the authorization server accept. I can imagine that if I have both an OAuth server and a SPIFFE deployment, I would be OK to say "I trust the SPIFFE deployment, and accept all the trust relationships it establishes" - it's a risk decision that is deployment specific.

A better way to address this is to highlight the risk that a SPIFFE deployment may contain multiple federation relationships, and as a result, the OAuth deployment SHOULD make a conscious decision on whether to allow federation. The riskd ecision belongs to the deployment.
Add a sentence on why - e.g. the iss claim points to a SPIFFE issues and cannot normally be resolved or something similar.

In this document, WIT-SVIDs are the SPIFFE variant of the WIMSE Workload Identity Token (WIT) as defined in {{?I-D.draft-ietf-wimse-workload-creds}} and make use of concepts defined in OAuth 2.0 Attestation-Based Client Authentication {{?I-D.draft-ietf-oauth-attestation-based-client-auth}}.

* The authorization server MUST bind the authenticated client to a registered client identifier. Specifically:

  * When a `client_id` parameter is present in the request, the authorization server MUST verify that it identifies the same registered client as the SPIFFE ID in the WIT-SVID `sub` claim. If this check fails, the authorization server MUST reject the authentication request.

pulls.title: Add section for interoperability between authorization servers and clients
pulls.author: stianst

comments.body:
@stianst - this text puts the burden for interoperability on the client. One of the guiding ideas behind OAuth was to try and absorb as much complexity in the server, especially the authorization server, as this is easie to maintain and there are fewer of them, making deployment easier.

What are your thoughts on putting a MUST on the AS to support both credential types instead offputting the burden on the client? Was the idea here that in a SPIFFE deployment a workload can easily obtain both?

Supporting both on the client side is fairly straightforward, while on the authorization server side it may be a lot more complicated, especially X509-SVIDs. Keycloak for instance supports JWT-SVID, but X509-SVID is on hold for now as it's a lot more effort to support.

There may also be policies in place on the authorization server side that determines which of the two should be used.

I don't think this is very different to what is common for discover endpoints; servers advertise a range of options they support, while clients need to adapt to that to select what works and what doesn't. In general client libraries need to support a wider range of capabilities compared to authorization servers to guarantee compatibility.

It's not just the server support, but also the infrastructures. If the infrastructure terminates TLS prior to reaching the server, it doesn't work from the client perspective even if the server supports it in theory.

Maybe it's worth to make it more clear that the deployment matters too?

```suggestion
It is the responsibility of the client to select the authentication method supported by the authorization server and its deployment.
```

Thanks for the clarification @stianst, it makes sense. @arndt-s I think the suggestion is good. Perhaps capturing some of this reasoning around TLS termination would be helpful for implementer as well as an implementation note (possibly through a separate issue)?

The values `spiffe_jwt` / `spiffe_x509` used in `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported` are not defined anywhere else in this document and are not covered by the current IANA considerations. Either use existing registered auth method values (e.g., `private_key_jwt`, `tls_client_auth`) or define these new method names and add the necessary IANA registrations. Also, `should` here is lowercase and reads like a non-BCP14 keyword; consider using `SHOULD` if this is intended to be normative.
```suggestion

The methods supported MUST be advertised in the authorization servers metadata {{RFC8414}} by including the corresponding registered values (e.g., `private_key_jwt` and/or `tls_client_auth`) in the `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported` list. These two consecutive sentences are duplicative and partially inconsistent; keep a single sentence here to avoid confusion about whether deployment-specific constraints are in scope for the client’s selection logic.
```suggestion
Clients are responsible for selecting, from among the authentication methods advertised by the authorization server, one that they support.
```

I can see a potential security issues with relying on `iss` field:

A trust relationship is configured in the authorization server for a given SPIFFE Trust Domain and it's associated SPIFFE Bundle Endpoint, but there is no explicit `iss` configured for this trust relationship. This would enable an attacker to craft a JWT-SVID with the `iss=https://attacker`; if the authorization server now validates the `sub` and SPIFFE Trust Domain it may blindly retrieve the keys from the `iss` without further verification.

To mitigate this it would be good to state the authorization server MUST only use iss-based discovery if the `iss` is known and associated with the SPIFFE Trust Domain.

In terms of the actual keys presented listed in OpenID Connect Discovery or OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata they may be advertised for other purposes than JWT-SVID; rather hypothetical but imagine a scenario where the provider is both an OpenID Connect provider and a SPIFFE provider, and a client can be registered with custom client-ids. Someone can then create a  client with `client_id=spiffe://mytrustdomain/myclient` and obtain an access token through an authorization request to then leverage this access token as a JWT-SVID.

The implementation in Keycloak avoids these issues completely by effectively always ignoring the `iss`.

Thanks @stianst - very helpful - I think these should be captured as security considerations. I think there are two issues here:

1. Trusted issuer
2. keys used for other purposes than issueing SVIDs that are published at the OpenID Connect metatadata point.
